## pqac-00000033

From text 'ballato2024prospectsandchallenges pages 4-6'.

J. Ballato, Peter D. Dragic, and Michel J. F. Digonnet. Prospects and challenges for all-optical thermal management of fiber lasers. Jan 2024. URL: https://doi.org/10.1088/1361-6463/ad1ddc, doi:10.1088/1361-6463/ad1ddc. This article has 33 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt is relevant to comparing air and water cooling and to understanding heat dissipation in fiber lasers, but it does not provide specific industrial operating-temperature limits, high-ambient-temperature derating curves, or a direct wall-plug-efficiency calculation. It identifies forced-convective heat exchangers using air or liquid water as the most common active cooling methods. Water cooling offers substantially greater heat-transfer capability: typical convective heat-transfer coefficients are approximately 100 W m−2 K−1 for flowing air and above 1000 W m−2 K−1 for flowing water. Thus, water can remove heat more effectively for a comparable thermal interface and temperature difference, although the article notes that active cooling introduces mechanical movement—such as fans or flowing water—that can fail and may generate vibrations affecting laser phase through the photoelastic effect. The article also emphasizes that minimizing heat generation is preferable to relying solely on cooling. Heat can impair active-ion spectroscopy, damage protective fiber coatings, produce thermal lensing and transverse mode instability, and increase frequency, phase, and intensity noise. The power-budget discussion indicates that coupling, combining, insertion, quantum-defect, and spontaneous-emission losses contribute to dissipated heat, but the excerpt does not explicitly equate these losses with wall-plug efficiency or specify temperature-based power derating.

## pqac-00000034

From text 'nemova2024briefreviewof pages 2-4'.

Galina Nemova. Brief review of recent developments in fiber lasers. Applied Sciences, 14:2323, Mar 2024. URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/app14062323, doi:10.3390/app14062323. This article has 83 citations.

The excerpt identifies the quantum defect—the energy difference between pump and laser photons—as an unavoidable source of heat in optically pumped fiber lasers. Part of the pump energy becomes phonons rather than photons, reducing conversion efficiency and creating thermal loads. The resulting heating can cause transverse-mode instability, thermal lensing, and catastrophic fiber damage, making heat management a key limitation on scaling fiber-laser output power. The article models steady-state heat conduction using the temperature, thermal conductivity, and dissipated heat density, with continuity conditions at the core-cladding boundary and heat transfer at the outer cladding boundary. Temperature depends strongly on pump evolution along the fiber. With forward pumping, the highest temperature occurs near the input side of the cavity, where signal amplification and phonon generation are strongest. Two-end pumping produces a more even axial temperature distribution, with maxima at both ends. Radial temperature variation is described as more uniform than axial variation and may be neglected when axial heat flow dominates. Photodarkening is another thermal concern because structural color-center formation increases background absorption and produces excess heating. The excerpt does not specify air-versus-water cooling, wall-plug efficiency values, industrial operating-temperature limits, or high-ambient-temperature derating criteria.

## pqac-00000035

From text 'ballato2024prospectsandchallenges pages 1-3'.

J. Ballato, Peter D. Dragic, and Michel J. F. Digonnet. Prospects and challenges for all-optical thermal management of fiber lasers. Jan 2024. URL: https://doi.org/10.1088/1361-6463/ad1ddc, doi:10.1088/1361-6463/ad1ddc. This article has 33 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt establishes the basic thermal-management context for fiber lasers but does not provide specific comparisons of air cooling versus water cooling, wall-plug efficiency values, industrial operating-temperature limits, or high-ambient-temperature derating rules. Fiber lasers are comparatively easier to cool than bulk lasers because their thin, coilable geometry provides a high surface-area-to-volume ratio. Nevertheless, heat generation remains particularly problematic at high power and must be managed in practical systems, potentially undermining reductions in size, weight, and power consumption. The article proposes an all-optical approach in which fiber materials and laser physics manage heat internally, with the potential to improve performance while reducing system size, weight, power consumption, and cost. The principal intrinsic heat sources identified are quantum defect (QD) and non-radiative relaxation. QD is the energy difference between pump and laser emission, generally released as heat, and is unavoidable for optical gain. It is expressed as QD = 1−(λp/λs), and typical values range from approximately 5%–8% for Yb3+ to nearly 60% for Er3+. These points are relevant to heat dissipation and efficiency, but the supplied pages do not quantify wall-plug efficiency or define temperature derating behavior.

From text 'ballato2024prospectsandchallenges pages 17-18'.

J. Ballato, Peter D. Dragic, and Michel J. F. Digonnet. Prospects and challenges for all-optical thermal management of fiber lasers. Jan 2024. URL: https://doi.org/10.1088/1361-6463/ad1ddc, doi:10.1088/1361-6463/ad1ddc. This article has 33 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt emphasizes that thermal management is central to the development of high-power and low-noise fiber lasers, amplifiers, and sensors. It presents anti-Stokes fluorescence (ASF) cooling as an internal optical cooling method that may reduce, but not necessarily eliminate, dependence on flowing-water cooling systems. The article anticipates that continued advances in ASF cooling, including improved ytterbium-doped fibers with near-100% quantum efficiency and higher quenching concentrations, could enable athermal fiber lasers and amplifiers when combined with suitable fiber and laser designs. The excerpt also notes that internally generated heat in active devices can alter refractive index and waveguide length, causing resonance-frequency fluctuations, output instability, increased noise, and sensor drift; internal ASF cooling could reduce these errors. However, this passage does not provide quantitative comparisons between air cooling and water cooling, wall-plug-efficiency values, heat-dissipation rates, industrial operating-temperature limits, or high-ambient-temperature derating specifications.

## pqac-00000037

From text 'ballato2024prospectsandchallenges pages 8-9'.

J. Ballato, Peter D. Dragic, and Michel J. F. Digonnet. Prospects and challenges for all-optical thermal management of fiber lasers. Jan 2024. URL: https://doi.org/10.1088/1361-6463/ad1ddc, doi:10.1088/1361-6463/ad1ddc. This article has 33 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt discusses anti-Stokes fluorescence cooling and its application to fiber lasers, with implications for heat dissipation in air. Cooling demonstrations commonly use vacuum chambers to minimize convective heat transfer from warmer air and achieve larger negative temperature changes. For practical fiber systems, however, operation in air is preferable, which introduces continuous heat input from the surrounding environment and reduces the achievable cooling effect. Fiber cooling is also less effective than cooling bulk crystals because the doped core must cool the inert cladding, fiber glasses generally support lower rare-earth concentrations than crystalline hosts, and single-mode fibers have smaller cores. The maximum extracted heat depends on the doped core area, active-ion concentration, radiative lifetime, and the ratio of emission to absorption cross sections at the pump wavelength. The excerpt gives a local heat-extraction expression based on excited-state population and radiative lifetime, and emphasizes that net thermal behavior is the balance between pump energy injected into the fiber and fluorescence energy removed. It does not provide information about water cooling, wall-plug efficiency, industrial operating-temperature limits, or high-ambient-temperature derating. It also does not specify a practical maximum temperature for industrial fiber lasers.

## pqac-00000038

From text 'zervas2014highpowerfiber pages 14-15'.

Michalis N. Zervas and Christophe A. Codemard. High power fiber lasers: a review. IEEE Journal of Selected Topics in Quantum Electronics, 20:219-241, Sep 2014. URL: https://doi.org/10.1109/jstqe.2014.2321279, doi:10.1109/jstqe.2014.2321279. This article has 1614 citations and is from a domain leading peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt provides limited but relevant information on thermal management in high-power fiber lasers. It states that power scaling in Nd3+ and Er3+/Yb3+-doped systems is constrained by their relatively large quantum defect and associated thermal-management requirements. Thermal effects are also linked to transverse mode instability (TMI): efficient fiber cooling substantially raises the TMI threshold in the cited PCF-SAT configuration. The review explains that all-fiber MOPA systems can use multiple pump-injection points to distribute pump absorption and thermal load more evenly, supporting reliable, service-free industrial operation. The excerpt reports that fiber lasers achieve wall-plug efficiencies above 30%, with expected lifetimes of approximately 100,000 hours based on single-emitter diode pumps, along with maintenance-free operation. It does not provide a comparison of air cooling versus water cooling, specific coolant architectures, industrial operating-temperature limits, ambient-temperature derating curves, or quantitative heat-dissipation values. Consequently, it supports general statements about the importance of cooling, thermal-load distribution, efficiency, and reliability, but cannot substantiate detailed claims about high-ambient operation or temperature-dependent power derating.

## pqac-00000039

From text 'ballato2024prospectsandchallenges pages 15-17'.

J. Ballato, Peter D. Dragic, and Michel J. F. Digonnet. Prospects and challenges for all-optical thermal management of fiber lasers. Jan 2024. URL: https://doi.org/10.1088/1361-6463/ad1ddc, doi:10.1088/1361-6463/ad1ddc. This article has 33 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt concerns all-optical anti-Stokes fluorescence (ASF) cooling as an internal thermal-management method for fiber lasers and related optical components. It suggests that radiation-balanced fiber lasers could potentially approach kilowatt output, with higher power possible if the fiber is allowed to operate moderately above room temperature and an external cooler removes the remaining heat load. Combining multiple lasers might extend total output toward 100 kW, although radiation balancing a single fiber at 100 kW is considered questionable with current silica technology. Fiber design is important: excessive cladding thickness can reabsorb escaping fluorescence and create additional heating, presenting a scaling challenge above approximately 10 kW. Exact room-temperature operation is not required; cooling the core to a few kelvin or about 20 K above ambient may be adequate. ASF removes heat at the core, potentially faster than conventional external cooling. For Yb-doped silica, ASF may enable pulse rates up to about 1 kHz, compared with a few hundred hertz or less for external cooling, because external heat diffusion through glass takes several milliseconds. The passage does not provide a direct air-versus-water cooling comparison, wall-plug-efficiency figures, industrial operating-temperature limits, or explicit high-ambient derating curves.

Abstract:
A finite element–based thermomechanical modeling approach is developed in this study to provide a prediction of the mesoscale melt pool behavior and part-scale properties for AlSi10Mg alloy. On the mesoscale, the widely adopted Goldak heat source model is used to predict melt pool formed by laser during powder bed fusion process. This requires the determination of certain parameters as they control temperature distribution and, hence, melt pool boundaries. A systematic parametric approach is proposed to determine parameters, i.e., absorption coefficient and transient temperature evolution. The simulation results are compared in terms of morphology of melt pool with the literature results. Considering the part-scale domain, there is increasing demand for predicting geometric distortions and analyzing underlying residual stresses, which are highly influenced by the mesh size and initial temperature setup. This study aims to propose a strategy for evaluating the correlation between the mesh size and the initial temperature to provide correct residual stresses when increasing the scale of the model for efficiency. The outcomes revealed that the predicted melt pool error produced by optimal Goldak function parameters is between 5 and 12%. On the part-scale, the finite element model is less sensitive to mesh size for distortion prediction, and layer-lumping can be used to increase the speed of simulation. The effect of large time increments and layer lumping can be compensated by appropriate initial temperature value for AlSi10Mg. The study aids practitioners and researchers to establish and validate design for additive manufacturing within the scope of desired part quality metrics.

Abstract:
Tailoring heat treatments for Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF) processed materials is critical to ensure superior and repeatable material properties for high-end applications. This tailoring requires in-depth understanding of the LPBF-processed material. Therefore, the current study aims at unravelling the threefold interrelationship between the process (LPBF and heat treatment), the microstructure at different scales (macro-, meso-, micro-, and nano-scale), and the macroscopic material properties of AlSi10Mg. A similar solidification trajectory applies at different length scales when comparing the solidification of AlSi10Mg, ranging from mould-casting to rapid solidification (LPBF). The similarity in solidification trajectories triggers the reason why the Brody-Flemings cellular microsegregation solidification model could predict the cellular morphology of the LPBF as-printed microstructure. Where rapid solidification occurs at a much finer scale, the LPBF microstructure exhibits a significant grain refinement and a high degree of silicon (Si) supersaturation. This study has identified the grain refinement and Si supersaturation as critical assets of the as-printed microstructure, playing a vital role in achieving superior mechanical and thermal properties during heat treatment. Next, an electrical conductivity model could accurately predict the Si solute concentration in LPBF-processed and heat-treated AlSi10Mg and allows understanding the microstructural evolution during heat treatment. The LPBF-processed and heat-treated AlSi10Mg conditions (as-built (AB), direct-aged (DA), stress-relieved (SR), preheated (PH)) show an interesting range of superior mechanical properties (tensile strength: 300–450 MPa, elongation: 4–13%) compared to the mould-cast T6 reference condition.

Abstract:
<jats:p>The influence of base plate temperature (25, 100, 200, and 400 °C) on the laser powder bed fusion processing of EN AW 7075 was systematically investigated using microstructural characterisation (LM, SEM, EBSD, GROD), chemical analysis, hardness testing, and thermal simulations across a broad range of process parameters. Moderate preheating at 100 °C and 200 °C showed no significant reduction in crack density or changes in grain morphology compared to processing without preheating. At the highest studied temperature—400 °C—a transition to columnar crack networks was observed, accompanied by modified grain orientation, pronounced stress relaxation, and reduced hardness. Independent of preheating temperature, consistent evaporation of Zn (~1 wt.%) and Mg (~0.3 wt.%) occurred during processing. Thermal simulations qualitatively supported the experimental observations, indicating increased thermal retention and displacement with increasing preheating temperature. The results demonstrate that base plate preheating alone is insufficient to suppress hot cracking in EN AW 7075 and may promote alternative crack-growth mechanisms at elevated temperatures, highlighting the need for alternative alloy or process design strategies.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Fabrication of high strength aluminum alloys using laser-based powder bed fusion (L-PBF) encounters challenges, including the occurrence of solidification cracks and the loss of volatile elements, such as Zn and Mg. The current work developed a Si-modified Al7075 alloy aiming at introducing eutectic phases to mitigate the solidification cracking during L-PBF. Based on Kou’s model, the addition of Zn and Mg decreased the crack susceptibility from 6504 °C to 5966 °C, and the addition of 3.74 wt pct of Si further decreased the crack susceptibility to 3960 °C. The Al7075 alloy fabricated by L-PBF exhibited a large amount of solidification cracks extending throughout the sample. Crack-free samples with a relative density of 99.94 pct, as inspected by X-ray microcomputed tomography, were achieved for the developed Si-modified Al7075 alloy. The microstructure showed a transition from a coarse columnar microstructure to a refined mixed columnar + equiaxed microstructure after alloy modification, with a concomitant grain size reduction from 59.0 ± 42.2 to 15.0 ± 9.4 µ m. Moreover, Si, Mg 2 Si, and Al 2 Cu phases were detected in the Si-modified Al7075 alloy. After a direct ageing heat treatment, the Si-modified Al7075 alloy showed minimal age hardening effect with a peak hardness of (146 ± 3 Hv).

Abstract:
<jats:p>Laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) of AA7075 is severely constrained by a narrow process window and susceptibility to defect formation (hot cracking and porosity), which often dominates performance. In this study, 5 wt.% AlCoCrFeNi2.1 high-entropy alloy (HEA) particles, volumetric energy density (VED = 74–222 J·mm−3), and subsequent T6 heat treatment were systematically investigated to reveal their combined effects on defect structure, crystallographic texture/substructure, and tensile behaviour. Quantitative EBSD shows a measurable grain refinement in the as-built state (average grain size 13.44 → 11.80 µm, ~12%) accompanied by a pronounced weakening of the <001> fibre texture (maximum MRD 4.94 → 2.38), indicating disrupted epitaxial growth and a more dispersed orientation distribution. After T6, the reinforced alloy retains a higher low-angle boundary fraction (31.62% vs. 24.17% in unreinforced AA7075) and a higher kernel average misorientation (0.80° vs. 0.60°), consistent with particle-stabilised substructure retention and retarded recovery. Across all VEDs, AA7075-HEA exhibits higher microhardness (compared with AA7075, the addition of HEA increases the hardness by roughly 20–50 HV) and tensile strength, with the intermediate VED (140.74 J·mm−3, T6 states) yielding the best performance. While macroscopic cracking is not fully eliminated, the results clarify that HEA-enabled texture/substructure modifications can contribute to enhanced defect tolerance and are more effectively translated into tensile performance when the as-built defect severity is controlled. These findings provide quantitative insights into defect–microstructure–property coupling in LPBF AA7075-HEA composites from as-built to T6 states.</jats:p>

Abstract:
High-performance engineering alloys, such as 7000 series aluminum alloys, suffer poor printability in laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) additive manufacturing. An enormous challenge lies in the suppression of solidification cracks caused by solidification shrinkage and thermal stresses. Porosity formation, as one of the main concerns for LPBF application, should also be avoided at the same time. In this study, aluminum alloy (AA) 7075 with and without Zr modification was additively manufactured by LPBF. Processing parameters of laser power and scanning speed, resulting in various volumetric energy density (VED), were experimentally determined to produce crack-free components with tailored microstructure. Optical microscopy was used to reveal how the crack density and porosity vary with VED. Scanning electron microscopy and transmission electron microscopy uncovered the detailed microstructure in the molten pool and the evolution of the elemental Zr addition. The results indicate that 1 w.t.% addition of elemental Zr in AA7075 led to lower crack density compared with 0.3 w.t.% addition. In 1 w.t.% Zr-modified AA7075, crack-free components were obtained under high VED. Fine equiaxed grains, instead of large columnar grains, were formed at the bottom of the molten pool boundary due to the existence of Al3Zr compound, which favored the nucleation of aluminum grains and elimination of cracks. The phenomenon of silicon segregation near cracks remained in Zr modified alloys, although its effects on cracking were suppressed. Spherical pores in the Zr-modified AA7075 increased due to the deterioration of fluidity by unmelted particles, which distracted the Marangoni flow as well. Sufficient laser energy input can increase the viscosity and ease the pores escaping. By optimizing parameters, crack-free AA7075 parts with low porosity can be manufactured through LPBF with Zr addition.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Fabrication Additive des Alliages d’Aluminium 6061 et 7075 avec Fusion Laser Sélective</jats:title>
                <jats:p xml:lang="fr">Actuellement, le défi auquel fait face le procédé SLM pour les alliages d'aluminium à haute résistance ou durcis par précipitation (séries 2xxx, 6xxx et 7xxx) est qu'ils sont sujets à la fissuration à chaud lors de la phase finale de solidification. Cela entraîne un grand nombre de fissures dans les échantillons imprimés. De plus, les éléments à bas point de fusion (Zn, Mg) de ces alliages ont tendance à s'évaporer facilement pendant le processus, entraînant des déficiences de composition qui affectent considérablement leurs propriétés mécaniques. Par conséquent, aborder les problèmes de fissuration et d'évaporation des éléments lors du processus d'impression SLM des alliages d'aluminium de résistance moyenne et élevée est une priorité de recherche majeure. L'objectif de cette étude est d'utiliser un équipement SLM à laser vert pour imprimer des échantillons d'alliage d'aluminium 6061 et 7075 sans fissures et d'étudier leurs propriétés mécaniques. Comparé aux lasers infrarouges traditionnels, la poudre d'alliage d'aluminium a un taux d'absorption plus élevé pour les lasers verts, ce qui signifie que des densités d'énergie plus faibles peuvent être utilisées pour l'impression. Cela réduit l'évaporation des éléments faiblement alliés. De plus, des particules de Ti et des particules de TiC/SiC sont ajoutées comme agents de nucléation pour affiner les grains et réduire les fissures. Trois types de poudres ont été préparés par mélange mécanique : 6061 + particules de Ti, 7075 + particules de Ti, et 7075 + particules de TiC/SiC. Les échantillons ont été imprimés en utilisant un équipement à laser vert, différent du laser infrarouge traditionnel.La morphologie et la composition en phases des poudres et des pièces imprimées ont été observées et étudiées à l'aide de la microscopie optique (OM), de la microscopie électronique à balayage (SEM) et de la diffraction des rayons X (XRD). Les mécanismes de renforcement et les propriétés mécaniques des échantillons imprimés ont été analysés en utilisant la microscopie électronique en transmission à haute résolution (HRTEM), la diffraction des électrons rétrodiffusés (EBSD), des tests de microdureté et des équipements de test de traction. En optimisant les paramètres de procédé (puissance laser, vitesse de balayage) et la proportion de particules ajoutées, des alliages d'aluminium 6061 et 7075 sans fissures ont été finalement préparés, et leurs mécanismes de renforcement ont été révélés. Cela offre une nouvelle approche pour le procédé SLM afin de produire des alliages d'aluminium haute performance sans fissures. Les résultats expérimentaux indiquent que pendant le processus d'impression laser vert avec des taux d'absorption plus élevés, une densité d'énergie de 52,1 à 62,5 J/mm³ est suffisante pour obtenir des échantillons imprimés relativement denses. Les grains dans les échantillons d'alliage d'aluminium 6061 et 7075 imprimés étaient de gros grains colonnaux (12,1-17,9 microns). L'ajout de particules de titane a considérablement affiné les grains, les transformant en grains colonnaux et équiaxes de petite taille (0,9-1,63 microns). En plus de servir de points de nucléation, les particules de titane ont réagi avec la matrice d'aluminium pour former Al3Ti, ce qui a été confirmé dans le HRTEM des impressions 6061 et dans le XRD des impressions 7075. L'ajout de particules de titane a donné des échantillons sans fissures pour les deux alliages 6061 et 7075. Comparé au laser infrarouge traditionnel, la perte des éléments Mg et Zn a été réduite avec le laser vert, et les propriétés de traction ont été améliorées. La limite d'élasticité des alliages 6061 traités thermiquement avec une teneur en Ti de 1% a répondu aux normes de la AA6061 forgée, et l'allongement a atteint 12,6%. La résistance à la traction du 7075 approchait également les 400 MPa, bien qu'une amélioration supplémentaire de l'allongement soit nécessaire.</jats:p>

## pqac-00000040

From text 'velikajne2026influenceofbase pages 1-2'.

Nejc Velikajne, Jožef Medved, Črtomir Donik, and Irena Paulin. Influence of base plate preheating on laser powder bed fusion–processed en aw-7075 aluminium alloy. Materials, 19:970, Mar 2026. URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/ma19050970, doi:10.3390/ma19050970. This article has 2 citations.

The excerpt reports that EN AW 7075 processed by laser powder bed fusion undergoes consistent alloying-element loss during processing: approximately 1 wt.% Zn and 0.3 wt.% Mg evaporate. This evaporation was independent of the investigated base-plate preheating temperatures (25, 100, 200, and 400 °C), indicating that preheating did not substantially prevent composition changes caused by laser-induced melt-pool temperatures. The loss of Zn and Mg is important because these elements affect phase equilibria, precipitation kinetics, strengthening response, solidification behaviour, and defect formation. Regarding cracking, moderate preheating at 100 °C and 200 °C did not significantly reduce crack density or alter grain morphology compared with no preheating. At 400 °C, the crack morphology changed to columnar crack networks, alongside modified grain orientation, pronounced stress relaxation, and reduced hardness. Thermal simulations indicated greater thermal retention and displacement as preheating temperature increased. Overall, base-plate preheating alone did not suppress hot cracking in EN AW 7075 and, at elevated temperature, may promote alternative crack-growth mechanisms. The excerpt therefore supports the conclusion that preheating changes thermal and stress conditions but does not eliminate Zn/Mg evaporation or reliably resolve the alloy’s intrinsic hot-cracking susceptibility.

At 400 °C, however, the cracking behavior changes substantially: distinct columnar crack networks form and cracks propagate along the build direction. The excerpt provides the experimental and numerical conditions relevant to studying heat accumulation during LPBF, but it does not include the later results quantifying temperature increase over build layers or substrate-temperature drift. The model accounts for repeated heating: while scanning layer n, the preceding two layers (n−1 and n−2) are also exposed to the heat source. The simulated base plate (region C) starts at the 100 °C preheating temperature, while the surrounding powder and base-plate-related initial region are otherwise described as initially at 37 °C ambient conditions; the surrounding powder is treated as a heat sink. Experiments used 316L powder in an SLM280HL system with a 100 °C preheating temperature and three inter-layer times: short, 18 s; intermediate, 65 s; and long, 116 s. Temperature was monitored using an off-axis MWIR camera at 600 Hz, with emissivity corrections for 316L surfaces and powder. The reported experimental values are preheating temperatures measured on a freshly recoated powder surface immediately before the next laser exposure, averaged over an 11 × 11 pixel central area. Thus, this excerpt supports analysis of inter-layer-time effects and measurement methodology, but it does not mention thermocouples, scan-area fraction, or actual measured temperature drift across the build.

## pqac-00000049

From text 'bugatti2024predictingtheroughness pages 2-3'.

Matteo Bugatti and Bianca Maria Colosimo. Predicting the roughness of overhanging surfaces in laser powder bed fusion via in-situ thermal imaging. Journal of Manufacturing Processes, 124:1340-1348, Aug 2024. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jmapro.2024.06.050, doi:10.1016/j.jmapro.2024.06.050. This article has 23 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt describes heat accumulation in laser powder bed fusion through in-situ high-speed MWIR thermal imaging rather than thermocouple measurements. Temperature histories of overhanging surfaces are collected and combined with ex-situ surface-quality measurements to model how geometry and process conditions affect external roughness. The experiments vary overhang angle, material, laser power, and laser mode. Because the overhang geometry causes the scanned area and scanning-vector length to increase at each layer, the total time needed to scan the parts also increases. Nevertheless, the interlayer dwell time remains approximately 28–30 seconds for every layer, since it is governed by the constant recoating-cycle duration. The authors specifically state that this consistent dwell time prevents interaction and heat accumulation across multiple layers. Thus, the excerpt supports analysis of layer-wise thermal behavior and the effects of scan-area growth, but it does not report substrate thermocouple data, measured build-plate temperature drift, or a quantitative temperature increase over the build. It frames thermal signatures as explanatory variables for surface quality and as a basis for predicting roughness under unseen process conditions.

From text 'maddison2022insitumonitoringand pages 170-176'.

G Maddison. In-situ monitoring and control during laser powder bed fusion of nickel superalloys. Unknown journal, 2022.

The excerpt provides limited but relevant information on substrate-temperature effects and thermal accumulation in LPBF. Six CM247-LC tiles were monitored in situ with a high-speed thermal camera to study how substrate heating affects the cooling rate of deposited material. The build began with the substrate at room temperature for several millimetres of build height, establishing a representative material base. After pausing the build, the substrate temperature was increased by 200°C and held at the target temperature for 20 minutes before resuming a single layer and collecting thermal images. This procedure was repeated in 200°C increments up to 1200°C, the maximum safe heater temperature. The experiment was intended to characterize cooling of bulk material under increasingly heated-substrate conditions. The excerpt does not report quantitative temperature drift across successive build layers, interlayer-time comparisons, scan-area fraction effects, or thermocouple measurements showing temperature accumulation during ordinary printing. It does mention that substrate temperature was controlled using the Aconity control thermocouple, but no thermocouple trend data are presented here.

The excerpt is directly relevant to heat accumulation in LPBF, particularly the influence of inter-layer time (ILT) and volumetric energy density (VED). It describes a finite-element model for 316L stainless-steel LPBF that simulates heat accumulation in a cuboidal build and compares the predictions with experimental results. The study identifies ILT as the duration between laser energy input at the same x–y location in successive layers, making it a geometry- and timing-dependent process parameter. The introduction cites prior work concluding that increasing ILT decreases heat accumulation; longer delays allow more cooling between successive layer exposures. The article also states that ILT and VED have a significant effect on heat accumulation and that the validated model can support optimization of processing parameters and geometries. However, this excerpt does not provide the requested quantitative temperature increase over build layers, thermocouple measurements in the build plate, or an explicit discussion of scan area fraction. It only establishes the general relationship between layer timing, energy input, build geometry, and thermal accumulation. Abstract

AlSi10Mg manufactured by laser powder bed fusion (or selective laser melting) benefits from a

very fine microstructure that imparts significant mechanical strength to the material compared to

the cast alloy. The build platform temperature stands out as a significant processing parameter

influencing  the  microstructure as  it  affects  the cooling  rate and thermal gradient during

manufacturing. Setting the build platform temperature to 200°C yields a negligible residual stress

level. However,  the strength  is lower compared to  that obtained using a  build platform

temperature of 35°C, with a similar fracture strain. A detailed 3D microstructural analysis

involving focused  ion beam/scanning  electron microscopy tomography was performed  to

describe the connectivity and size of the Si-rich eutectic network and link it to the strength and

fracture strain. The coarser microstructure of the 200°C build platform material is more prone to

damage. The α-Al cells as well as the Si-rich precipitates present a larger size in the 200°C

material, the latter thus having a lower strengthening effect. The Si-rich eutectic network is also

less interconnected and has a larger thickness in the 200°C material. An analytical model is

developed to exploit these microstructural features and predict the strength of the two materials.

1. Introduction


The relatively novel additive manufacturing (AM) area represents a great potential for various

applications and industries, but  it also involves important scientific challenges. In the case of

metal AM,  its attractiveness  is important  in structural applications  for the aeronautic and

aerospace  industries. AM aluminium  alloys  are  specially  interesting  in  these  lightweight

applications, laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) AlSi10Mg being a common material and process

combination [1-3]. Note that selective laser melting remains a rather common trade name for the

LPBF technology.


There  is a strong demand  for high performing structural parts  that can allow  for  further

improvements, leading to decrease in weight and fuel consumption. AM can be a powerful tool in

this endeavour, but, in order to represent a significant and highly attractive leap forward, its

design flexibility has to be accompanied by an enhancement in mechanical performance. To

achieve this, a thorough understanding from the materials science point of view of the AM parts

has to be acquired [4].


In fact, various research efforts have been devoted to lightweight metal AM, with a focus on

Ti6Al4V and AlSi10Mg. The latter is a very good example of the AM potential which has

already found its application in the aeronautic industry. The technology allows to produce unique

complex lattice structures and the material exhibits very good static mechanical performance [5].

Compared to the same alloy produced by casting, the LPBF counterpart offers an improvement of



                                          2167% in mechanical strength and of 74% in ductility (for a build platform temperature of 35°C

for the LPBF material); see Fig. 1, which reports the tensile stress - strain curves for as cast and

as built LPBF AlSi10Mg. The high cooling rate of the LPBF process yields a totally different and

much finer microstructure than casting [6].


The tensile properties are known to be affected by the LPBF processing parameters [7]. In

particular, here it is found that with a build platform temperature of 200°C the fracture strain is

not improved while the strength is significantly decreased; see Fig. 1. This difference deserves

some in-depth analysis to  relate  it to the microstructural features and in particular to the

strengthening Si-rich network, which has been found to be the main damage initiation site [8].

Considering practical applications, the use of a higher build platform temperature is still relevant,

since the part presents almost no residual stresses, while they were found to reach 50 MPa in

tension with a 35°C build platform temperature. These residual stress levels were measured in

previous work [9] for identical samples as the ones for which the mechanical properties are

provided in Fig. 1.


Previous studies have investigated the microstructure and the mechanical behaviour of LPBF

AlSi10Mg manufactured with build platform temperature of 35°C or 200°C separately, but the

comparative  investigation  of  both  materials  to  determine  the  differences  between  the

microstructures and their origin and relation to the mechanical behaviour is very limited. Awd et

al. [10] have studied the mechanical behaviour of LPBF AlSi10Mg fabricated with build platform

temperatures of 35°C and 200°C. Their research nearly exclusively focused on the fatigue aspects

and was thus mainly aimed at the influence of porosity. Indeed, the effect of porosity is more

critical than that of the microstructure in cyclic loading regime. Buchbinder et al. [11] revealed

degraded mechanical properties of LPBF AlSi10Mg with a build platform temperature of 220°C.


                                          3However the microstructure was not thoroughly characterised. It is therefore pertinent to address

the microstructural aspects and their variation with the build platform temperature, especially

with the aim of unveiling the origin of the static mechanical behaviour observed in Fig. 1.


Regarding the microstructure of LPBF AlSi10Mg,  it is now well established [12,13] that  it is

composed of an α-Al  cellular phase and a  Si-rich eutectic phase. This microstructure  is

sometimes called “pseudoeutectic” [13] due to its metastability and to the far from equilibrium

conditions at which it is originated. Indeed, the LPBF process is characterised by very fast and

local heating, which is followed by rapid cooling and solidification under high thermal gradient

[14] leading to a very fine metastable microstructure. The build platform temperature can have an

impact on the thermal gradient during the cooling down of the  material, influencing the

microstructure. Due  to  the  layer by  layer  building  strategy,  the  microstructure of LPBF

## pqac-00000059

From text 'wartbichler2022laserpowderbed pages 2-4'.

Reinhold Wartbichler, Tobias Maiwald-Immer, Fabian Pürstl, and Helmut Clemens. Laser powder bed fusion of intermetallic titanium aluminide alloys using a novel process chamber heating system: a study on feasibility and microstructural optimization for creep performance. Metals, 12:2087, Dec 2022. URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/met12122087, doi:10.3390/met12122087. This article has 8 citations.

The excerpt describes the preheating requirements and hardware of a high-temperature EOS LPBF system for processing crack-sensitive TiAl alloys. Conventional industrial LPBF machines generally provide base-plate heating from approximately 200 °C to 500 °C, but this is insufficient because TiAl processing requires constant, elevated temperatures and the base-plate preheating effect diminishes as build height increases. The EOS-M290-HT is presented as a modified EOS-M290 system with a high-temperature process chamber. Its base plate can be heated to 900 °C, while the uppermost powder-bed layer can reach 1200 °C. The machine also incorporates process-chamber cooling, inert-gas purification to maintain oxygen levels below 200 ppm, process monitoring, sensors, an IR camera, and data logging. The excerpt further notes that inductively heated baseplates have enabled preheating temperatures up to 1000 °C in previous LPBF studies. It does not describe an Aconity machine, Renishaw or Trumpf TruPrint heated build modules, or water cooling or piston cooling. The cooling explicitly mentioned is cooling of the process chamber using inert gas. Thus, the passage supports temperature ranges and inert-gas chamber-cooling details, but not a direct comparison among the named commercial systems.

## pqac-00000060

From text 'rothfelder2023abriefhistory pages 10-11'.

Richard Rothfelder, Florian Nahr, Lova Chechik, Dominic Bartels, and Michael Schmidt. A brief history of the progress of laser powder bed fusion of metals in europe. Journal of Manufacturing Science and Engineering, Aug 2023. URL: https://doi.org/10.1115/1.4062788, doi:10.1115/1.4062788. This article has 17 citations.

The excerpt describes the development and purpose of heated platforms in laser powder bed fusion of metals (PBF-LB/M). Commercial machines commonly provide baseplate preheating up to 500 °C, while higher-temperature systems require machine components capable of operating under elevated thermal loads. An early study by Hagedorn et al. used approximately 1,600 °C to manufacture crack-free oxide ceramic parts; however, the resulting reduction in melt viscosity negatively affected contour resolution. This work helped motivate further research into high-temperature preheating and contributed to the creation of Aconity 3D, whose customized machines can provide platform preheating above 1,000 °C. For carbon-enriched H11 tool steel, Bischoff et al. used a commercially available SLM 280 equipped with a heating system capable of 500 °C and found that increasing preheating substantially reduced cracking and final-part distortion. Huber et al. likewise reported benefits from 500 °C platform preheating. The excerpt does not provide information about a 200 °C platform, water cooling, piston cooling, or heated build modules from Renishaw or TRUMPF TruPrint systems.

The excerpt does not describe an Aconity, Renishaw, or Trumpf TruPrint machine, nor does it mention water cooling or piston cooling. It describes the EOS-M290-HT prototype’s LPBF heating system for TiAl alloy processing. The machine can heat its base plate to up to 900 °C, while a separate VCSEL-based system heats the uppermost powder-bed layer, or process zone, to as much as 1200 °C. An infrared camera measures the powder-bed surface temperature, and a dynamic control system maintains a homogeneous, constant temperature during scanning. The system is intended to reduce distortion, residual stress, and cracking, while making material quality less dependent on build height. Each newly recoated layer can be heated homogeneously without separate preheating or post-heating steps, while retaining productivity and build rates comparable to a standard LPBF machine. Thus, the excerpt provides a relevant example of a high-temperature LPBF platform and layer-heating architecture, with temperature capabilities that overlap the requested 200–1000 °C range, but it does not provide specifications for the named commercial machines or identify any cooling method.

Abstract:


In this study, single line scans at different laser powers were carried out using selective laser

meting (SLM) equipment on a pre-fabricated porous Al86Ni6Y4.5Co2La1.5 metallic glass (MG)

preform. The densification, microstructural evolution, phase transformation and mechanical

properties of  the scan  tracks were  systematically  investigated.  It was found  that  the

morphology of the scan track was influenced by the energy distribution of the laser beam and

the heat transfer competition between convection and conduction in the melt pool. Due to the

Gaussian distribution of laser energy and heat transfer process, different regions of the scan

track experienced  different thermal  history,  resulting  in a gradient microstructure and

mechanical properties. Higher laser powers caused higher thermal stresses, which led to the

formation of cracks; while low power reduced the strength of the laser track, also inducing

cracking. The thermal fluctuation at high laser power produced an inhomogeneous chemical



                                     1distribution which gave rise to severe crystallization of the MG, despite the high cooling rate.

The crystallization occurred both within the heat affected zone (HAZ) and at the edge of melt

pool. However, by choosing an appropriate laser power crack-free scan tracks could be

produced  with  no  crystallization.  This  work  provides  the  necessary  fundamental

understanding that will lead to the fabrication of large-size, crack-free MG with high density,

controllable microstructure and mechanical properties using SLM.


Keywords: Selective laser melting; Metallic glass; Solidification microstructure; Phase

transformation; Mechanical properties





                                     21. Introduction


As a newly emerging additive manufacturing (AM) technique, selective laser melting (SLM),

has undergone a rapid development for a decade  [1].  It  is becoming one of the most

promising manufacturing techniques in the world to fabricate fully dense metal components

without the need for tooling, machining or time-intensive post-processing [1]. Using a high

power laser as the energy source, SLM fabricates metal components in a layer-wise manner

by a complete melting and solidification mechanism. The complete melting differentiates

SLM from other widely used AM techniques, e.g. direct metal laser sintering (DMLS) [1]. In

SLM, the geometry of each layer is defined based on a computer aided design (CAD) model.

Then the laser is scanned across the powder bed to selectively melt powder particles, which is

followed by rapid solidification. After one layer is built, the build platform descends by the

layer thickness (typically 50 - 100 µm) and a new layer of powder is deposited on top. During

scanning of the each layer, the previously processed layer experiences surface remelting,

resulting in the consolidation of adjacent powder layers. This process repeats until the entire

metal component  is finished. SLM has been used to fabricate a wide range of metal

components including some non-ferrous metals such as Al, Ti and Ni alloys, which have

potential applications in biomedical implants, automobile and aircraft industries [2-5].


Unlike conventional subtractive manufacturing techniques, SLM possesses many advantages

such as fabrication of metal components with complex geometries free of expensive moulds,

high materials usage efficiency together with near-net-shape formation and recycling of

unmelted powder [1]. In addition, customer-designed one-off fabrication process and the

production of components with different geometries in one batch are possible. Due to the

high energy and the small spot size of the laser beam, only a tiny volume of material


                                     3undergoes the heating, melting and subsequent rapid solidification. This induces an extremely

high temperature gradient within the material, strong thermal fluctuation in the melt pool and

local shrinkage. These cause considerable accumulation of thermal  stresses within the

components which can give rise to micro- and macro- cracks, curling or even delamination [6,

7].


The  first Al-based metallic glass (MG) was discovered in late 1980s and has attracted

increasing attention due to its high specific strength and low cost in comparison to other MG

materials [8]. However, due to its low glass forming ability (GFA) and thermal stability, it

has taken more than two decades to fabricate the  first 1 mm diameter Al-based MG

(Al86Ni6Y4.5Co2La1.5,  in  at. %) by copper mould casting  [9]. This  size  limitation has

constrained further investigation and improvement of the mechanical properties, especially

the room temperature plasticity, greatly hindering the practical application of Al-based MG

materials. Although in recent years there have been several reports of the fabrication of Al-

based MG materials with diameter larger than 1 mm through hot compressing and spark

plasma sintering (SPS) [10, 11], their shape and size are constrained by the die and only some

simple components have been produced. More importantly, the tailoring or controlling of

microstructure during such processes is extremely difficult [12, 13].


Following the concept of rapid heating and cooling a small volume of materials each time,

SLM can potentially provide an alternative manufacturing method for producing large size

and complex geometries from MG powder. This “point-by-point” manner may also enable

the microstructure to be tailored, resulting in the formation of gradient microstructure. This

heterogeneous microstructure has been reported to improve the plasticity in some MG

materials [14-17]. However, SLM  is a complex technique which involves complicated

physical and chemical processes during fabrication. Some preliminary results have been

reported on fabrication of Fe-based MG scaffolds using SLM, but there were problems with

                                     4low-density and cracking [18]. The stability, temperature gradient and thermal fluctuation in

and near the melt pool have a great influence on the microstructure of final components [1].

and near the melt pool have a great influence on the microstructure of final components [1].

The microstructure and properties of final components can be influenced by many other

factors. Some factors are SLM-related such as laser power, laser spot size, scanning speed,

scanning strategy and layer thickness. Others are materials-related such as reflectivity, heat

conductivity and specific heat capacity [1]. When considering Al-based MG, their brittleness,

low GFA and thermal stability, make the fabrication process even more complicated. The

phase transformation (or retention of the amorphous phase) within Al-based MG during SLM

can be influenced by the cooling rate and heat affected zone (HAZ). The brittleness and

possible  devitrification  of Al-based MG  will  increase  the  risk of  cracking, which  is

detrimental to the densification and mechanical properties of final components. However, it

appears that nothing has been published regarding the processing, microstructure evolution

and mechanical properties of Al-based MG materials processed using SLM.


In this work, we have systematically studied the densification, microstructure evolution and

mechanical properties of an Al-based MG material processed using single line scans at

different laser powers. The structure of the melt pool and HAZ and their relation to phase

transformation have been assessed. The underlying mechanisms for the microstructural

evolution,  including  crack  formation and  mechanical  properties  variation, have been

explained. The aim of this work  is to  first demonstrate the feasibility of fabrication of

marginal Al-based MG using SLM and then to establish the relationship between laser power

and microstructure and mechanical properties of Al-based MG. These would further provide

necessary fundamental basis for the fabrication of other MG materials using SLM.





                                     52. Experimental procedures


2.1 Powder material


An  Al-based MG  powder  with  a  spherical  morphology  and  a  composition  of

Al86Ni6Y4.5Co2La1.5 (in at. %) was used for this investigation. Master ingot with a nominal

composition of Al86Ni6Y4.5Co2La1.5 (in at. %) was first prepared by arc melting high-purity

elemental pieces Al (>99.9 wt. %), Ni (>99.9 wt. %), Y (>99.0 wt. %), Co (>99.9 wt. %) and

La (>99.0 wt. %) under a Ti-gettered argon atmosphere for six times to ensure chemical

homogeneity. Then the powder was fabricated from this master ingot through gas atomisation

in high-purity nitrogen at the Institute of Metal Research, Chinese Academy of Sciences,

Shenyang. Powder particles were sieved and X-ray diffraction (XRD, D/max III, Cu Kα

target, operated at 40 kV and 60 mA with a step size of 0.02 ° and scanning speed 2 °/min)

was used to analyse the phase formation of the sieved powder with different diameters. To

ensure fully amorphous nature, only powder particles with a diameter below 25 µm were

used [19].


2.2 SLM process


SLM experiments were conducted using a ReaLizer SLM-100 machine (ReaLizer GmbH,

Germany) which is equipped with a fibre laser, generating a laser beam with a wavelength of

1060 nm and maximum power of 200 W at the part bed. The intensity of the laser beam can

be considered to have a Gaussian distribution and the laser beam scanning can be assumed to

be continuous [20].


An Al substrate (125 mm × 125 mm) is fixed on the working platform and kept at room

temperature. The chamber was purged with high-purity argon gas to reduce the oxygen

content to ≤ 1000 ppm.

Where P  is the laser power, v is the laser scan speed, d  is the spot size of the laser beam

and W  is the thickness of the powder layer. To avoid the interference between multiple laser

scan tracks and to investigate the interaction between laser beam at different laser powers and

the Al86Ni6Y4.5Co2La1.5 MG powder particles, only a single line scan was performed at each

condition. According to several preliminary trials, the scanning velocity was fixed at 1000

mm/s, while the laser powers were set to be 80, 120, 160 and 200 W.


If a single line scan was conducted on loose Al86Ni6Y4.5Co2La1.5 MG powder spread on the

substrate,  it was not possible to remove the samples off the substrate without damage.

Therefore, the powder was lightly consolidated into a bulk form with very low density (≤ 75 %

measured by the Archimedes method and close to the tap density) using SPS (SPS-1030

model, SPS SYNTEX INC, Japan) and a tungsten carbide (WC) die (outer diameter 30 mm,

inner diameter 10 mm and height 20 mm). To ensure low density and avoid devitrification

during SPS, a low pressure of 200 MPa and a sintering temperature of 238 °C (which is 30 °C

below the powder’s glass transition temperature [19]) were used without any isothermal

holding. The very low density of the preform meant that it was analogous to the loose powder

normally used in SLM.


2.3 Microstructure characterisation and mechanical properties


Microstructure evolution, melt pool and HAZ of the Al86Ni6Y4.5Co2La1.5 MG processed by

SLM were characterised using scanning electron microscopy (SEM, Zeiss 1555 VP-FESEM,

operated at an accelerating voltage of 15 kV and working distance 10 mm). The SEM

                                     7samples were prepared in the X-Y (horizontal) and Z (vertical) cross-section (see Fig. 1). The

samples were polished following the standard polishing procedures and carbon coated before

SEM observation.

Nanoindentation (Hysitron® Triboindenter) was used to measure the hardness and elastic

modulus of the SLM processed Al86Ni6Y4.5Co2La1.5 MG samples at room temperature in air

with a Berkovich indenter of a tip radius of 100 nm. Samples were polished but uncoated.

The measurements were conducted on both the X-Y and Z cross-sections along different

directions within the melt pool. The nanoindentation tests were made under the load control

mode. The maximum indentation force applied was 2 mN at a rate of 200 µN/s for both

loading and unloading. The dwell time was fixed at 10 s. Elastic modulus of the samples was

calculated using the Oliver-Pharr method [22]. A minimum of 7 indentations were conducted

on each site.

3.1 Microstructure and phase transformation


As a layer-wise fabrication technique, SLM fabricated components are expected to show

different microstructures between the horizontal (X-Y cross-section, perpendicular to the

building direction) and vertical (Z cross-section, parallel to the building direction) planes (see

Fig.  1). To study the microstructure and phase transformation of the SLM processed

Al86Ni6Y4.5Co2La1.5 MG, SEM back scattered images (BSE) of the scan tracks within X-Y

cross-section and Z cross-section were taken and are shown in Figs. 2 and 3, respectively.


It can be seen in Fig. 2 that the width and morphology of the scan tracks (X-Y cross-section)

vary with the laser power. On increasing laser power from 80 W to 200 W, the width of the

which is a consequence of the higher laser energy density according to Eq. 1. The scan tracks

also show different morphologies  at the different laser powers. As the laser power  is

form at a power of 160 W, but these are now only vertical and parallel to the scanning

      The sealing action of elastomeric seals is explained earlier in Section 2.1, through

the inverse hydrodynamic theory of lubrication. This phenomenon in conjunction with

hydrodynamic and elasto-hydrodynamic theories of lubrication is described in great detail

by various authors in their works [63], [64], [65], [83], [84], [85], [86], [87], [88], [89]. With

that being said, there is significant room for improving the understanding around the

dynamic sealing mechanism, even after research of nearly three quarters of a century

[70], [90].


      Because of how lubrication is achieved, i.e. the role of surface asperities as well

its dependence on speed, based on Equation 2.1, parametric studies relating to wear and

friction are necessary. Unfortunately, analytical solutions to this equation are difficult.

Experimental studies for hydraulic oil by Rana et al. [64] using a seal on plate rig reveal

that friction has a direct correlation with surface roughness. However, friction does not

reduce further after a certain level of surface finish on the steel plate is achieved.

Irrespective of seal surface finish, any roughness on the steel plate increases friction

      Change in mechanical properties of elastomers as a result of permeation is an

area of research interest [67]. Theiler et al. [92] in their static high pressure testing of

hydrogenated NBR with hydrogen at 100 MPa and 120oC noticed a loss in tensile strength

and elongation at break. However, this degradation was found to be temporary with the

properties  reverting  to  their  original  level 48  hours  post-exposure.  Comparative

experiments with nitrogen resulted in no considerable reduction in these properties,

making the effect of hydrogen more important. This is attributed to how hydrogen places

itself between the elastomer matrix and fillers, impairing their strengthening effect. In

another experiment carried out by Yamabe and Nishimura [72] with sulfur-vulcanized NBR

filled with either carbon black or silica revealed a clear decrease in the tensile elastic

modulus of the samples. For the non-filled and carbon black filled samples, this was

attributed to fluid uptake and hence a decrease in cross-linking density of the elastomer.

The true fracture stress for the filled samples also showed a negative correlation with

increased swelling. It was also noticed that higher tensile strength of the filled samples

resulted in lower swelling.

50 bar and 150oC for 10, 30 and 100 days (±1/2 days). They found that specimens of

unexposed samples, and EPDM exposed for 99 days still had a lower hardness than its

unexposed counterpart. They attributed this result to the deterioration of bonding strength

caused by hydrogen-induced  swelling. EPDM,  despite  having a somewhat  high

permeability, was found to be the most mechanically stable, while HBNR degraded

considerably and FKM showed poor decompression resistance despite presenting good

This metastable polarization is based on the magnetic hysteresis of the material. The
hysteresis phenomenon is discussed in more detail in Section 2.1. The hysteresis behavior
of the NdFeB material, however, depends on the microstructure of the material. In Section

polarization losses and some design issues are discussed.

2.1    Analysis of hysteresis in NdFeB type materials

Hysteresis is the dependence of a system not only on its current environment but also on its
past. The state of the magnetization in magnetic materials  is thus dependent on the
magnetizing history. Changing external magnetic field forms metastable magnetic states in
the material. Return of the material to the original state requires energy input.

The hysteresis phenomenon in this chapter is discussed from the permanent magnet point
of view and  especially considering  the behavior of  sintered NdFeB based magnet
materials. The special characteristics of soft magnetic materials are excluded from the
discussion.

2.1.1  Hysteresis loop

Fig. 2 illustrates the hysteresis behavior of a permanent magnet material. The vertical axis
shows the magnetization state of the material and the horizontal axis represents the
external magnetic field. At location 1 (hereafter loc. 1), the material is non-magnetized in
zero external field. As the external magnetic field is increased, the magnetization of the
material  is also increased (loc. 2), but not linearly. Magnetization increases until the
                                 14saturation state is reached (loc. 3). After that, the magnetization is not increasing anymore.
If the external field is then decreased, the magnetization remains close to the saturation
level. Even at the point where the external field has disappeared (loc. 4), the remanent
magnetization of the material is close to the saturation level. This magnetization state at
zero external magnetic field (after saturation) is called the remanence (Br) of the material.

In NdFeB materials the magnetization state remains close to the remanence even when the
external magnetic field is increased in the reverse direction. At location 5, demagnetization
of the magnet begins. As the reverse field is increased to the coercivity (Hci) level (loc. 6),
the macroscopic magnetization of the material has disappeared. Magnetization in the
reverse direction starts to increase as the reverse field is further increased. At location 7,
the saturation is achieved in the reverse direction.





Figure 2.      Schematic presentation of a hysteresis loop of a permanent magnet material.


The key properties of permanent magnets are thus the remanence, Br, which determines the
magnetic  field produced by a given volume of magnetic material, and the  intrinsic
coercivity, Hci, the material’s resistance to demagnetization [6].

The theory of the hysteresis phenomenon is divided into three classes: rate-independent
hysteresis, rate-dependent hysteresis, and thermal relaxation [2]. The rate-independent
hysteresis does not include any time-dependent effects and it assumes that every B/H point
describes the equilibrium  state. Thermal  effects are ignored  in the rate-independent

                                 15hysteresis model, and it is therefore a zero temperature approximation. The rate-dependent
hysteresis includes some dissipation mechanisms, such as eddy currents, which limit the
rate at which the system can respond to the external field. Hysteresis loops increase in area
with increasing field rate of change [7]. This is due to the shift of coercivity (loc. 6) to the
left.

Thermal relaxation causes the system to approach thermodynamic equilibrium by thermal
fluctuations. The thermal relaxation will shift the coercivity (loc. 6) of the rate-independent
hysteresis to the right. Magnetic viscosity results from the thermal relaxation, and the
phenomenon is discussed in more detail in Section 2.1.4.

Permanent magnet design usually relies on the rate-independent hysteresis theory even
though it is precise only at 0 K. Thermal effects are considered only by measuring the M
vs. H curves at different temperatures. Measured curves are assumed to present the
equilibrium states at these temperatures. Permanent magnets are usually operated between
loc. 4 and 5 in Fig. 2, and this part of the hysteresis is expected to be independent of the
field rate of change. Magnetic viscosity  is often considered to be so small that the
approximation of rate-independent hysteresis can be safely adopted [7].

Hysteresis loops are measured by hysteresis-graphs, which are presented in more detail in
Section 3.2.

function.arguments:
{"answer": "## Literature Review: Thermal Management Considerations for a Research LPBF Machine with Heated Interchangeable Build Modules for Aluminium Alloys

### 1. Measured Build-Plate and Part Temperature Rise from Laser Heat Input

The most systematic quantitative study of laser-induced heat accumulation in LPBF was conducted by Chaudry et al. (2022) on 316L stainless steel cuboidal specimens built in an SLM 280HL with a 100 °C platform preheat. Using mid-wave infrared thermography, they measured the temperature at the top of the freshly recoated powder surface at the end of each inter-layer time (ILT). The results demonstrated that ILT is the dominant variable controlling heat accumulation:

- **Short ILT (18 s):** The preheating temperature rose from the 100 °C set point to approximately **545 °C** at the top of the 70 mm build, with a steep initial gradient that decreased as convective and conductive losses grew (pqac-00000056, pqac-00000057).
- **Medium ILT (65 s):** The maximum temperature reached approximately **230 °C** (pqac-00000057).
- **Long ILT (116 s):** The temperature stabilised near **170 °C**, indicating that an approximate equilibrium between energy input and dissipation had been reached (pqac-00000057).

Volumetric energy density (VED) also matters: at short ILT, increasing VED from 49 to 82 J/mm³ raised the peak temperature further, demonstrating that higher laser power and slower scan speeds compound the heat accumulation problem (pqac-00000057). The build platform acts as the principal heat sink during early layers, with an effective conductive heat-transfer coefficient on the order of 1000 W/(m²·°C) in modelling studies (pqac-00000001). As build height increases, the growing thermal resistance between the scan plane and the cooled platform reduces its heat-sink effectiveness, so accumulation accelerates if ILT is too short (pqac-00000051).

For aluminium alloys on small platforms—the scenario of your machine—the thermal situation is qualitatively similar but potentially more severe because aluminium's high thermal conductivity draws laser heat rapidly into the platform, while the small module thermal mass limits its heat-storage capacity. Heugue et al. (2026) reported that large A357 funnel-shaped specimens built on a Nikon NXG12 SLM600 (12 lasers, 650 W each, 150 °C platform) experienced such severe heat accumulation at approximately mid-height that surface blistering occurred and the build had to be stopped (pqac-00000055). This demonstrates that even at a modest 150 °C set point, dense, poorly ventilated geometries on a heated platform can locally reach temperatures well above 230 °C (pqac-00000006). On your Ø25 mm module with only 30 W conductive loss at 200 °C and an estimated 80–110 W time-averaged laser input, the net surplus of 50–80 W into a very small thermal mass will produce measurable drift within tens of layers unless active cooling or longer ILTs are used.

### 2. How Commercial and Research LPBF Machines Manage Platform Heat

**Platform preheating capabilities.** Standard commercial LPBF systems commonly provide resistive baseplate preheating up to approximately 200–500 °C (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000060). The SLM 280 platform (SLM Solutions/Nikon) is available with up to 500 °C preheating, and this was used to substantially reduce cracking and distortion in carbon-enriched H11 tool steel (pqac-00000060). Aconity 3D has developed customised machines with platform preheating above 1000 °C, originally motivated by processing of oxide ceramics at ~1600 °C (pqac-00000060). The EOS M290-HT prototype combines a 900 °C resistively heated baseplate with a VCSEL-based upper-powder-layer heater capable of 1200 °C, controlled via infrared camera and dynamic feedback, with process-chamber cooling provided by purified inert gas (pqac-00000059, pqac-00000061).

**Heat removal approaches.** The peer-reviewed literature is notably sparse on the mechanical details of how heat is removed from the piston or build cylinder in commercial machines. The build platform is universally recognised as the primary heat-extraction path: conduction through the substrate, into the piston head, and ultimately into the machine frame (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000001). The Maddison (2022) thesis on an Aconity system mentions a control thermocouple for substrate temperature, implying closed-loop baseplate heating control (pqac-00000050). In standard machines operating at modest temperatures (≤200 °C), natural conduction to the machine body and the inert-gas atmosphere appears to be the dominant cooling mechanism, supplemented by ILT-based thermal management. Where higher temperatures are used, the EOS-M290-HT explicitly incorporates process-chamber cooling via inert gas flow (pqac-00000059). Water-cooled pistons, build cylinders, and cold plates are described in manufacturer technical documentation and patent literature but are rarely detailed in peer-reviewed journal papers. For your design, the 30–97 W steady-state loss predicted by your FE model at 200 °C is insufficient to reject the 80–110 W of time-averaged laser input; active cooling (water channels in the piston head or cylinder wall) or deliberate ILT extension will be essential.

**Interlayer dwell as a thermal management strategy.** The Chaudry et al. (2022) results demonstrate that increasing ILT from 18 s to 116 s can reduce peak temperature from 545 °C to 170 °C under identical power and VED conditions (pqac-00000057). Bugatti and Colosimo (2024) noted that a constant ~28–30 s recoating dwell was sufficient to prevent cross-layer accumulation in their builds on an EOS system (pqac-00000049). Extending ILT is therefore the simplest lever for your machine, though it reduces productivity.

### 3. Effects of Uncontrolled Platform Temperature Drift on Aluminium Alloys

#### AlSi10Mg and A357 (Al-Si-Mg): In-situ Ageing and Overageing

The Al-Si-Mg alloy system is acutely sensitive to the prolonged thermal exposure inherent in a heated-platform LPBF process. Bosio et al. (2021) systematically studied AlSi10Mg on platforms at 45, 100, 150, and 200 °C. At 150 °C, peak-age hardness of ~138.6 HV was reached in approximately 2.5 h of holding; builds exceeding ~13 h began to overage (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000004). At 200 °C, samples were already overaged after roughly 10 h of printing, with as-built hardness of only 100.5 ± 3 HV; 100 h isothermal treatment at 200 °C reduced hardness further to ~91 HV (pqac-00000003). At 250 °C, hardness fell below 80 HV, and distortion was essentially eliminated—but at the cost of severely degraded strength (pqac-00000005).

Macías et al. (2020) compared AlSi10Mg fabricated at 35 °C and 200 °C platform temperatures on an EOS M290. The 200 °C material exhibited significantly lower strength (while residual stress was negligible at ~0 MPa versus ~50 MPa at 35 °C). The Si-rich eutectic network was coarser, less interconnected, and more prone to damage initiation at 200 °C (pqac-00000058). The strength improvement of LPBF over cast AlSi10Mg was 167% at 35 °C but substantially less at 200 °C (pqac-00000058).

For A357 (AlSi7Mg0.6), Heugue et al. (2026) demonstrated that large-scale components on a Nikon NXG12 with a 150 °C platform experienced up to a **30% reduction in mechanical properties** in regions where heat dissipation was insufficient (pqac-00000008). Local temperatures exceeding approximately 230 °C caused hardness below 90 HV, interpreted as severe overageing with dissolution/coarsening of β″-Mg₅Si₆ precipitates and spheroidisation of the eutectic Si network (pqac-00000006). Post-build cooling contributed 15–35% of total equivalent ageing time, further exacerbating the problem (pqac-00000010).

Lehmhus et al. (2022) showed that stress-relieving AlSi10Mg at 350 °C/2 h reduced UTS to ~280 MPa at room temperature (versus ~450 MPa as-built at 35 °C), though the characteristic cellular microstructure was not completely destroyed (pqac-00000009).

**Implication for your design:** A drift from 200 °C to 290 °C over a 40 mm stroke with a few-hour build represents a worst-case overageing scenario for Al-Si-Mg alloys, transforming the as-built microstructure toward an overaged condition with potentially 30–50% loss in hardness and strength. Closed-loop cooling to hold the platform within ±10 °C of the 200 °C set point is therefore metallurgically necessary.

#### 7xxx and High-Strength Al-Zn-Mg(-Cu) Alloys: Evaporation and Cracking

For EN AW 7075, Velikajne et al. (2026) measured consistent evaporation of approximately **1 wt.% Zn and 0.3 wt.% Mg** during LPBF, independent of baseplate preheating temperature from 25 to 400 °C (pqac-00000040, pqac-00000041). This evaporation is driven by the extreme melt-pool temperatures (well above the ~907 °C boiling point of Zn and ~1090 °C for Mg) and is therefore essentially unaffected by substrate-level thermal management (pqac-00000043, pqac-00000047). Moderate preheating at 100–200 °C showed no significant reduction in crack density, while 400 °C promoted columnar crack networks and reduced hardness through stress relaxation and altered grain orientation (pqac-00000040, pqac-00000043). Stopyra et al. (2020) reported that AA7075 cracking was driven by microsegregation of Zn, Mg, Cu, and Si to grain boundaries and the low 338 °C eutectic temperature of the Al-Mg-Zn system (pqac-00000046). Preheating to 300 °C altered thermal gradients but did not change the solidification-crack fracture mode (pqac-00000046).

For high-solute Al-Zn-Mg alloys, Babu et al. (2020) reported vaporisation losses of ~2.21 wt.% Zn and ~0.2 wt.% Mg for Al-18Zn-4Mg, with fine vaporisation cracks observed (pqac-00000024). Zhou et al. No peer-reviewed papers were found that specifically document derating, failures, or ambient-temperature problems of LPBF-class (~200–1000 W) air-cooled single-mode fibre lasers in enclosed automated-storage environments.
